# OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
CUI//PROPIN

**Subject:** Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. d/b/a Z.ai (HKEX: 2513; registered name since 2025: Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited) — GLM-family large language models
**Transactions in scope:** (a) US persons' use of Z.ai hosted API services (api.z.ai; open.bigmodel.cn; ZCode cloud features); (b) distribution of open GLM weights through US-based model hubs and inference marketplaces; (c) integration of GLM models into US enterprise and government-facing software products.
**Prepared by:** OICTS Analytic Cell | **Date:** 9 October 2026 | **Product type:** Initial assessment, draft for interagency review (DoD/OUSD(I&S), DHS/CISA, ODNI, State/EB, Treasury/OIA)
**Handling:** CUI//PROPIN. Open-source reporting cited inline; internal exposure estimates are OICTS data-team products and are not releasable outside the enclave. Analyst draft only — decisions rest with the Executive Director and the Under Secretary. This product does not constitute a determination under 15 CFR part 791.

---

## Bottom Line Up Front

Zhipu AI is not an independent Chinese startup that happens to have state investors; it is a strategic asset of the Chinese party-state, incubated out of Tsinghua University, recapitalized in 2024–2025 almost entirely by PRC state capital, Entity-Listed in January 2025 for advancing the People's Liberation Army's military modernization, and now monetized on the Hong Kong exchange as the first of China's "AI tigers" to go public. Its flagship GLM models — released under the permissive MIT license and distributed at scale through US infrastructure, including Amazon Bedrock and Microsoft Foundry — are the leading edge of a deliberate Beijing strategy to make PRC-developed models the default substrate of global AI, including inside the US enterprise stack.

We assess that the hosted Z.ai API is an unacceptable data and access risk for any US person or organization handling sensitive data: the same serving infrastructure that silently suppresses answers on Tiananmen, Falun Gong, Tibet, and Xinjiang necessarily inspects every prompt, and Z.ai has already demonstrated covert collection of local user workspaces through its ZCode client. We assess that open-weight distribution is the more strategic of the two threats — less because we have evidence of malicious artifacts in the weights (we do not) than because it is irreversible, unauditable at scale, dependency-creating, and dual-use by design: the same open ChatGLM lineage that US developers download for cheap inference has been adapted by a PRC defense-industry institute into a patent for a military intelligence LLM covering the full intelligence cycle.

Monitoring alone would concede these risks. We recommend a prohibition-tier package now: an ICTS determination barring US-person transactions with Z.ai hosted endpoints, CISA direction and FAR clauses taking GLM/Z.ai out of federal use and federal-facing supply chains, and enforceable gating conditions on US hubs and inference providers that continue to distribute GLM weights commercially — with a conditional path for vetted, attested, pinned self-hosted weights in non-sensitive uses, and a full possession ban held in reserve.

---

## Key Judgments

1. **Zhipu functions as an instrument of PRC national strategy, not as an independent commercial actor — high confidence.** Formal ownership is founder-led (the CSRC IPO tutoring filing reports no controlling shareholder, with Tang Jie and Liu Debing as actual controllers), but control in the PRC system runs through state capital, government procurement, standards bodies, party-leader access, and law — not only equity. Zhipu raised more than RMB 4.8 billion (US$650M+) from PRC state and state-affiliated investors between December 2024 and April 2025 alone; OpenAI's June 2025 assessment pegged cumulative state-backed investment above US$1.4 billion. BIS determined in January 2025 that Zhipu and nine related entities "advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization."

2. **GLM technology demonstrably supports PRC military-intelligence capability — high confidence that PLA and PRC defense-industry elements have adapted Zhipu-derived models; moderate confidence that this occurs with Zhipu's knowledge and acquiescence.** A December 2024 patent application by a PRC state-owned defense-industry research institute describes a military LLM fine-tuned from ChatGLM (the Zhipu/Tsinghua open model family) and trained on OSINT, HUMINT, SIGINT, GEOINT, and TECHINT data to support "every phase of the intelligence cycle" and decision-making in military operations ([Recorded Future, June 2025](https://assets.recordedfuture.com/insikt-report-pdfs/2025/ta-cn-2025-0617.pdf)). Open weights are the enabling mechanism: the openness that makes GLM valuable to US developers is what makes it fine-tunable by the PLA.

3. **The Z.ai hosted API exposes US persons' prompts, documents, and code to PRC access, and applies CCP content controls in production — high confidence.** Independent testing shows GLM-4.7 answers only 45 percent (27/60) of FreedomBench's factual questions when served through Z.ai's own API — returning blank responses on Tiananmen, Falun Gong, Tibet, Xinjiang, and jailed-lawyer questions — while identical weights answer all 60 correctly on non-PRC hosts, and GLM-5.2 answers 30/60 through Z.ai versus 60/60 in an attested confidential-compute enclave ([TrustedRouter FreedomBench](https://trustedrouter.com/blog/censored-at-the-host-not-the-model)). Content-level suppression of that kind requires infrastructure that reads and filters requests in real time. Z.ai's contractual claims (Singapore processing via a wholly-owned PRC-parent subsidiary, Jingsheng Hengxing Technology Pte. Ltd.; "do not store any of the content"; no API retraining) are unaudited and would not survive PRC compulsory process under the National Intelligence Law (2017), Cybersecurity Law (2017), or Data Security Law (2021).

4. **Z.ai has already crossed the line from risk to demonstrated covert collection — high confidence.** In September 2026, developers found Z.ai's ZCode coding assistant silently packaging entire local workspaces (a 313MB encrypted archive; 564 failed upload attempts to Alibaba Cloud storage, plus a smaller package that succeeded) with no functional off-switch; the decryption key was held server-side by Z.ai, making deletion unverifiable. Z.ai apologized, attributed the behavior to a default-on "repository indexing" feature, and promised to open-source the ZCode codebase and admit third-party assessors ([SCMP, 20 Sep 2026](https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3368159/chinese-ai-firm-zai-faces-reputation-hit-after-users-spot-unauthorised-uploads); [The Register, 22 Sep 2026](https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/09/22/zai-says-sorry-for-slurping-up-your-code-open-sources-zcode/5298300)). A PRC robotics firm reportedly banned Z.ai tools internally after the disclosure.

5. **Open-weight distribution is a deliberate state-managed strategy, not a commercial afterthought — high confidence in the direction, moderate confidence in the specifics.** PRC-origin models grew from an estimated 1 percent of global AI workloads in late 2024 to roughly 30 percent by end-2025 ([House Homeland Security Committee, 29 Apr 2026](https://homeland.house.gov/2026/04/29/chairmen-garbarino-moolenaar-announce-joint-investigation-into-national-security-risks-posed-by-prc-ai-models/)), while Beijing simultaneously convened Alibaba, ByteDance, and Z.ai about restricting overseas access to China's top models, including potential criminal penalties under national-security law for model leaks ([Reuters, 7 Jul 2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/beijing-is-looking-curbing-overseas-access-chinas-top-ai-models-sources-say-2026-07-07/)). Beijing treats model distribution as a strategic export and will calibrate it to state advantage; the United States should not treat it as neutral commerce.

6. **We have no evidence of malicious artifacts in current GLM weights, and we cannot rule them out — moderate confidence in the negative finding, low confidence it will hold.** CISA reports no observed malicious behavior to date but flags that backdoors and data poisoning in open weights are hard to rule out (interagency input). GLM-5.x checkpoints are ~750B-parameter mixture-of-experts artifacts (~1.5TB in safetensors) that no practical audit can clear; provenance rests entirely on trust in a PRC vendor that has already demonstrated covert client-side collection. CAISI separately assesses GLM-5.3 as "the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date" — 40.4 percent success on vulnerability-discovery/exploit-development benchmarks against the 90.2 percent US frontier best ([NIST/CAISI, 17 Sep 2026](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/09/caisis-assessment-zais-glm-53-cyber-capabilities)) — meaning GLM distribution hands significant offensive cyber capability, ungated by any usage policy, to anyone who downloads it.

7. **US exposure is broad, commercially mainstreamed, and under-mapped — moderate confidence in magnitude (low-precision telemetry), high confidence in the trend.** OICTS data-team estimates for Q3 2026: ~2,300 US-origin organizations calling Z.ai endpoints (CDN telemetry, low precision); GLM weights mirrored on Hugging Face (zai-org) with >9M cumulative downloads across geographies; at least 9 US cloud marketplaces/inference providers serving GLM; GLM models identified in 41 US software products by SBOM sampling, of which 6 are federal contractors. Public corroboration: GLM-5 peaked at #2 on OpenRouter (Feb 2026, ~260B tokens/day at peak) and is served by 8+ live providers; GLM-5 and GLM-5.3 are first-party listings on Amazon Bedrock, and GLM-5.x is served through Fireworks on Microsoft Foundry — i.e., the two largest US cloud platforms now distribute Zhipu models by default to enterprise customers.

8. **Existing authorities do not reach the problem; the ICTS framework is the right instrument — high confidence.** Entity-Listing (Jan 2025) restricts exports *to* Zhipu with presumption of denial, but does not restrict US persons' use of Zhipu services. NDAA FY2026 §1532 covers DoD and its contractors only. EO 14409 (June 2026) hardens federal cyber defense and benchmarks "covered frontier models" but creates no restriction on PRC models in the civilian economy. No current instrument governs US private-sector hosted API use or marketplace distribution of PRC model weights. That is precisely the gap EO 13873 and 15 CFR part 791 exist to close.

---

## Subject Overview (ownership, funding, leadership)

**Corporate identity.** Zhipu was founded in Beijing in 2019 as a Tsinghua University spin-out from the Department of Computer Science's Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG), led by professor Tang Jie with co-founder Li Juanzi ([Reuters, 15 Apr 2025](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinas-zhipu-ai-takes-initial-steps-an-ipo-2025-04-15/)). It is one of China's six "AI tiger" startups. In 2025 it renamed itself Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited (北京智譜華章科技股份有限公司) for a Hong Kong listing, trades as HKEX: 2513, and operates internationally as Z.ai, with the international API hosted through Jingsheng Hengxing Technology Pte. Ltd., a Singapore company incorporated 23 November 2023 and an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of the PRC parent.

**Control.** Per the CSRC IPO tutoring filing (April 2025), Zhipu has **no controlling shareholder**; the **actual controllers are Tang Jie and Liu Debing**. Tang holds 7.41 percent directly; Liu holds 0.26 percent directly and, through holding platforms, controls 17.40 percent of voting rights; together with concert-party shareholders (Li Juanzi, Xu Bin, CEO Zhang Peng, and the Ningbo Huihui partnership) the block accounts for a further 12.16 percent of votes ([NBD, 15 Apr 2025](https://www.nbd.com.cn/articles/2025-04-15/3832254.html)). We flag this precisely because it is the wrong lens: the analytic question is not who holds equity but who can direct the company. On that question the record is one-directional.

**State capital.** Since 2023 Zhipu has been systematically capitalized by PRC state and state-affiliated entities: an RMB 2.5 billion round (2023) from Alibaba, Tencent, Meituan, Ant, Xiaomi, and HongShan; a US$400 million round (May 2024) joined by Saudi Prosperity7/Aramco at a ~US$3 billion valuation; an RMB 3 billion D+ round (December 2024); and, in March 2025 alone, more than RMB 1.8 billion from Hangzhou municipal investment funds (~RMB 1 billion), Zhuhai state conglomerate Huafa Group (RMB 500 million), and Chengdu High-Tech zone (RMB 300 million) ([Reuters, 3 Mar 2025](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinas-zhipu-ai-raises-137-million-state-funds-bet-ai-race-2025-03-03/); [Reuters, 19 Mar 2025](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinese-ai-firm-zhipu-raises-257-mln-state-backed-funding-spree-2025-03-19/)). The Beijing Artificial Intelligence Industry Investment Fund — a municipal state fund whose first large-model investment Zhipu was — added a further RMB 200 million in April 2025, explicitly citing Zhipu's open-weight strategy ([NCSTI, Apr 2025](https://www.ncsti.gov.cn/kjdt/xwjj/202504/t20250418_202045.html)). OpenAI's Global Affairs analysts assess total state-backed investment above US$1.4 billion and describe Zhipu as "backed by the Chinese Communist Party" ([OpenAI, 25 Jun 2025](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front); [CNBC, 26 Jun 2025](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/06/26/openai-flags-beijing-backed-zhipu-ai-as-a-top-rival.html)).

**Leadership and scale.** Executive directors as of the June 2026 board: Chairman Dr. Liu Debing, CEO Dr. Zhang Peng, Ms. Zhang Xiaohan; non-executive directors Dr. Li Juanzi, Mr. Li Jiaqing, Mr. Wang Meng; independent directors including Dr. Yang Qiang ([HKEX filing, 2 Jun 2026](https://www.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2026/0602/2026060200005.pdf)). More than 800 employees (2024), roughly 60–70 percent in R&D ([Turing Post profile](https://www.turingpost.com/p/zhipu)). Offices reported in Singapore, Malaysia, the United Kingdom, and the Middle East, plus US marketing presence (Z.ai showcased GLM-5.2 at AI Engineer World's Fair, San Francisco, June 2026).

**Listing and capital trajectory.** Zhipu completed HK IPO tutoring with CICC (April 2025), listed on HKEX on 8 January 2026 (US$558 million IPO; stock closed +13.2 percent on debut), rallied roughly 1,500 percent, and placed a further ~US$4.01 billion of shares in early July 2026 ([CNBC, 8 Jan 2026](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/08/china-ai-tiger-goes-ipo-zhipu-hong-kong-debut-openai-knowledge-atlas-hsi-hang-seng-listing.html); [Reuters, 8 Jul 2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/chinas-zhipu-ai-launches-4-billion-hong-kong-shares-offering-term-sheet-shows-2026-07-08/)). It is now the most valuable public AI pure-play in China (market cap ~US$62 billion, August 2026) and has proposed a Sci-Tech Board (STAR Market) A-share listing of 2–8 percent of its capital ([HKEX announcement, 1 Jun 2026](https://iis.aastocks.com/20260601/12182571-0.PDF)) — deepening, not reducing, its position inside the PRC capital account and regulatory perimeter.

**Products in scope.** The GLM family: GLM-130B (2022, first Chinese open 100B-class model), ChatGLM-6B (2023), GLM-4.x, GLM-4.5/4.6/4.7 (2025), GLM-5 (11 Feb 2026), GLM-5.2 (16 Jun 2026), GLM-5.3 (14 Aug 2026; weights released two weeks later), all open-weight under MIT license since July 2025; plus vision (GLM-4.5V/V series), the ZCode coding assistant, consumer app Qingyan (~25 million users), and the bigmodel.cn MaaS platform (~700,000 enterprise/developer accounts). GLM-4.6 was trained on PRC domestic chips (Cambricon) and GLM is advertised as compatible with Huawei Ascend; Zhipu bundles eight Huawei Ascend 910s in its "AI-in-a-box" private deployments ([NBR, 2024](https://www.nbr.org/publication/chinas-generative-ai-ecosystem-in-2024-rising-investment-and-expectations/)).

---

## Links to PRC Government / Military Entities

1. **Entity List designation for military modernization.** On 16 January 2025, BIS added Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. and nine related Zhipu entities to the Entity List (destination: China) because these entities "advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research," with a license requirement for all items subject to the EAR and a presumption of denial ([Federal Register, 16 Jan 2025](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-16/html/2025-00704.htm); [BIS press release](https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-makes-revisions-entity-list-strengthen-u.s.-national-security)). Zhipu publicly "strongly opposed" the designation ([Reuters, 16 Jan 2025](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinese-ai-related-firm-zhipu-says-strongly-opposes-inclusion-us-export-control-2025-01-16/)). This is a USG finding by the interagency End-User Review Committee, applying the "reasonable cause, specific and articulable facts" standard — not an allegation by a competitor.

2. **PLA adaptation of ChatGLM for military intelligence.** Recorded Future's Insikt Group assesses with high confidence that the PLA and PRC defense industry "very likely" use a mix of domestic LLMs — including Zhipu AI's — to build generative-AI intelligence tools, and documents a PLA/defense-industry patent (December 2024) describing a military LLM fine-tuned from **ChatGLM** (Zhipu/Tsinghua) on all-discipline intelligence data (OSINT, HUMINT, SIGINT, GEOINT, TECHINT) to support "every phase of the intelligence cycle" and decision-making in military operations ([Recorded Future, June 2025](https://assets.recordedfuture.com/insikt-report-pdfs/2025/ta-cn-2025-0617.pdf)). The open-weight strategy is the delivery mechanism.

3. **State procurement as a business model.** Zhipu's commercial base is ToG/ToB (government/enterprise) with heavy central-SOE and municipal concentration: a ~RMB 45.5 million Beijing E-Town "政务大模型" (government LLM) platform contract (June 2025); a ~RMB 61.28 million Hangzhou municipal city-projects deal (May 2025); China Oil & Gas Pipeline Network Group (国家管网) LLM/MaaS procurement at ~RMB 10.2 million; Suzhou Rail Transit AI consulting (~RMB 5.7 million); COSCO Shipping legal/risk-control base-model work; and Tsinghua logistics-industry LLM projects. Local state investors explicitly frame equity as market access — Chengdu's RMB 300 million is tied to building a Sichuan provincial base model ("Zhuge") on GLM ([Securities Times, 20 Mar 2025](https://stcn.com/article/detail/1598285.html)).

4. **Party-state integration.** OpenAI's analysts report that Zhipu leadership "frequently engages with CCP officials, including Premier Li Qiang," that Zhipu has "numerous government procurement contracts," and that it participates actively in setting **national AI technical standards** ([OpenAI, 25 Jun 2025](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front)). Zhipu's overseas expansion is synchronized with PRC foreign policy: sovereign-LLM infrastructure offers across Belt and Road/Digital Silk Road geographies (Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kenya), joint innovation centers, a Dubai "content-safety" lab, and Huawei-Ascend "AI-in-a-box" hardware — what Chinese state media themselves call "China's answer to OpenAI for Countries."

5. **Legal compulsion.** Zhipu operates under PRC law that compels assistance to state security organs (National Intelligence Law 2017, Art. 7; Cybersecurity Law 2017; Data Security Law 2021) and under the CAC's generative-AI regime, which requires content moderation, alignment with "socialist values," and security assessment. The company cannot lawfully refuse a state request, cannot notify users, and publishes no transparency reporting. Any assessment of Zhipu as a "private" counterparty must price this in.

---

## Data and Access Risk

**What US persons send.** Hosted API use transmits prompts, retrieved documents, source code, system prompts, tool outputs, and logs to Zhipu-controlled infrastructure. Enterprise coding/agentic use (GLM-5.x's core selling point) means entire codebases, tickets, credentials-in-context, and infrastructure descriptions flow to the provider. The compliance bar for US organizations is higher than commonly assumed: sending US-origin controlled technical data or EAR99 software source to an Entity-Listed party via its API is an export (see the compliance analysis of GLM-5.2's terms, [June 2026](https://weichen221.substack.com/p/the-glm-52-dilemma-compliance-challenges)), and API processing of US persons' personal data at scale implicates the DOJ's EO 14117 bulk-sensitive-data regime (28 CFR part 202).

**What Zhipu demonstrably does.** Two independent, public behavior sets establish more than theoretical risk:

- *Serving-layer inspection and censorship.* Z.ai's own flagship endpoints blank politically sensitive answers (GLM-4.7: 27/60 FreedomBench; GLM-5.2: 30/60) while identical weights answer fully elsewhere — including in an attested confidential-compute enclave where the operator provably cannot read or alter requests ([TrustedRouter](https://trustedrouter.com/blog/censored-at-the-host-not-the-model)). To suppress on those topics, the host must be reading prompts in production. A censorship pipeline and a monitoring pipeline are the same machine with different outputs.
- *Covert client-side collection.* ZCode staged silent, encrypted uploads of complete local workspaces to Alibaba Cloud storage (564 failed attempts observed for one user's 313MB archive; a smaller package succeeded), defaulted on with no off-switch, with the decryption key held only by Z.ai so that "deletion" could not be verified by the user ([SCMP, 20 Sep 2026](https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3368159/chinese-ai-firm-zai-faces-reputation-hit-after-users-spot-unauthorised-uploads); [TNW](https://thenextweb.com/news/zai-zcode-encrypted-upload-only-zai-can-verify)). This is not a hypothetical about what Beijing *could* make Zhipu do; it is a September 2026 record of what Zhipu *did*.

**Why contractual assurances fail.** The international API is nominally processed in Singapore by Jingsheng Hengxing Technology Pte. Ltd. — a wholly-owned indirect subsidiary of the Beijing parent, incorporated in 2023, on the eve of Zhipu's Entity-Listing — with a DPA asserting Singapore processing and non-retention of API content ([comparative API-privacy analysis](https://erkinekici.com/articles/comparing-llm-api-privacy/), which scores Z.ai "CAUTION" and DeepSeek "AVOID"). Z.ai publishes no SOC 2/ISO attestations, no independent audit of the Singapore infrastructure, no government-request transparency, and no warrant-canary. Under PRC law, the parent is compellable; a Singapore shelf entity does not interpose anything against the PRC state, and the mainland endpoint (open.bigmodel.cn) stores data in China outright. Absent classified information to the contrary (ODNI annex pending), we should assume prompt-level visibility and retention capability, because the observed censorship behavior already requires it.

**Residual risk even with perfect behavior.** Zhipu can change terms, endpoints, and model behavior unilaterally and remotely; enterprise "integration" products inherit updates and telemetry paths; and prompt content disclosed to Zhipu becomes PRC intelligence-accessible regardless of what Zhipu intends. For federal, defense-industrial, and critical-infrastructure users, this is a decision, not an oversight.

---

## Open-Weight Distribution Risk

**Scale.** GLM weights are published on Hugging Face under zai-org under the MIT license — free for commercial use, no use-policy enforcement mechanism. GLM-5 (11 Feb 2026; ~744B total / ~40B active parameters) shows ~2.1 million all-time downloads with ~815,000 in a recent 30-day window; GLM-5.3 (~753B total / ~40B active, 1M-token context) accrued ~1.8 million downloads within weeks of release ([Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5); [AWS Bedrock model card](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-card-zai-glm-5-3.html)). OICTS data team counts >9M cumulative downloads across zai-org repositories (all geographies). OpenRouter telemetry showed GLM-5 at **#2 platform-wide at its peak** (peak rank 14 Feb 2026; ~260.7B tokens/day peak) across 8+ live providers ([ArtifactHub](https://artifactshub.ai/zai-org/glm-5)).

**US distribution surface.** At least 9 US inference marketplaces/providers serve GLM per OICTS snapshot (OpenRouter-listed providers, Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Parasail, Baseten, and others); Cerebras, Novita, and Featherless serve it publicly. Most consequentially, **Amazon Bedrock lists GLM-5 and GLM-5.3 as first-party model cards available to "eligible enterprise customers,"** and **Microsoft Foundry serves GLM-5 via the Fireworks partnership** (public preview March 2026; GLM-5.3 Flash on AMD MI300X added October 2026). The two largest US cloud platforms have thus made a PRC Entity-Listed party's model a default enterprise offering. MIT licensing also means US products embed GLM without legal friction — our SBOM sampling found 41 of them, 6 federal contractors.

**Technical risk vectors, ranked:**

- *Unauditable artifacts.* A 750B-parameter model is ~1.5TB of opaque floats. No practical review can exclude latent triggers, poisoned behaviors, or silent capability changes between checkpoints; CISA assesses no malicious behavior observed to date but that backdoors/poisoning "are hard to rule out" (interagency input). Provenance rests entirely on trust in a vendor with a demonstrated covert-collection record.
- *Update and provenance drift.* Distribution through hubs and marketplaces means weights, adapters, quantizations, and system prompts evolve outside any US control point; hash-pinning is uncommon in enterprise practice. There is no mechanism to "recall" weights already downloaded by 41+ US products and thousands of organizations.
- *Offensive cyber capability, ungated.* CAISI assesses GLM-5.3 is the most cyber-capable open-weight model yet released (SEC-Bench Pro 40.4%, ExploitBench 61.1% best-of-three, vs. US frontier 90.2%/100%) ([NIST/CAISI](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/09/caisis-assessment-zais-glm-53-cyber-capabilities)). MIT licensing means anyone — hostile states, criminals, proxies — receives the capability with no usage policy, no gating, no logging.
- *Values and narrative alignment.* Federal testing cited by Congress found leading PRC models echo CCP-approved narratives at rates far exceeding comparable US systems ([House HS Committee, 29 Apr 2026](https://homeland.house.gov/2026/04/29/chairmen-garbarino-moolenaar-announce-joint-investigation-into-national-security-risks-posed-by-prc-ai-models/)). GLM's censorship sits in the serving layer (weights answer freely on neutral hosts), so US users of weights get an unaligned model rather than a censored one — but enterprise fine-tuning on GLM base models bakes PRC-corpora priors into products downstream, invisibly.
- *Strategic dependency.* Beijing is actively deliberating export controls over its top models — including with Z.ai at the table — and could degrade, withdraw, or condition GLM availability to extract leverage ([Reuters, 7 Jul 2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/beijing-is-looking-curbing-overseas-access-chinas-top-ai-models-sources-say-2026-07-07/); [FT via Reuters, 21 Jul 2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/china-considers-tighter-export-controls-ai-models-chips-ft-reports-2026-07-21/)). Every US product that hard-codes a GLM dependency imports that political risk into its roadmap. Beijing deciding what Chinese models may leave China, while Washington leaves distribution to market forces, is the asymmetry to correct.

**Dual-use reality.** The PLA's military-intelligence LLM patent is built on the same open ChatGLM lineage. Open-weight distribution is not merely a US consumer-good; it is PRC-origin capability delivered simultaneously to US enterprises and to PLA engineers, with the second effect impossible to prevent from the first.

---

## US Exposure

*OICTS data-team snapshot, 6 October 2026 (internal estimates; CUI//PROPIN; low precision where noted):*

- **Hosted API:** ~2,300 US-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026 (CDN telemetry from a cooperating provider; **low precision** — treat as an order of magnitude, not a census).
- **Open weights:** zai-org GLM repositories mirrored on Hugging Face; >9M cumulative downloads (all geographies); available through at least 9 US cloud marketplaces/inference providers; first-party listings on Amazon Bedrock and (via Fireworks) Microsoft Foundry; peak OpenRouter rank #2 platform-wide (Feb 2026).
- **Enterprise integration:** GLM identified in 41 US software products via SBOM sampling (coding assistants, customer-support bots, document processing); **6 of the 41 are federal contractors.**
- **Government surface:** DoD use is already prohibited by NDAA FY2026 §1532 (covered AI from DeepSeek/High Flyer, covered nations including the PRC, or covered companies; SecDef waiver authority) ([FY2026 NDAA §1532 text](https://agora.eto.tech/instrument/2694)). No equivalent restriction yet exists for civilian agencies or the broader federal contractor base — a gap this review should close.
- **Context:** PRC-origin models overall reached an estimated ~30 percent of global AI workloads by end-2025 (from ~1 percent in late 2024); congressional committees have opened investigations into PRC model adoption by US companies (Anysphere, Airbnb) and the OSTP formally characterized PRC distillation operations as "industrial-scale" campaigns (April 2026). Pending legislation (H.R. 10670) would bar "Chinese AI models" from federal devices and procurement.
- **Financial exposure:** US passive investors now hold HK-listed Zhipu (2513) paper via global indices/funds; a USG adverse determination would move a ~US$62 billion market cap and should be coordinated with Treasury.

---

## Mitigation Options / Recommended Measures

We assessed the full ladder from monitoring through prohibition. Trade-offs for each are set out in the companion product **`measures.md`**; summary:

1. **Monitoring only** — preserves optionality but concedes data access today and lets dependency deepen; we do not recommend it as the end state.
2. **CISA guidance + BOD (EO 14409 §2(c))** — fast, cheap, covers federal systems; leaves the private sector and marketplaces untouched.
3. **FAR/procurement bars** — removes GLM/Z.ai from federal-facing supply chains (extends §1532's logic to civilians); enforceable at contract level; does not reach purely commercial use.
4. **ICTS determination (15 CFR 791) prohibiting US-person use of Z.ai hosted endpoints** — the decisive step against the highest-confidence data risk; trade-off is cost to small US users and displacement to third-party mirrors, not elimination of the threat.
5. **Marketplace gating conditions** (attested serving, pinned hashes, no vendor telemetry, no Z.ai account linkage, contractual flow-downs) — the enforceable middle path for open-weight distribution; deliberately stops short of a possession ban.
6. **Supply-chain/CI prohibitions** — bar GLM in national-security systems and designated critical infrastructure; scope definitions are the hard part.
7. **Full prohibition including self-hosted weights** — reserved as escalation; State/EB is right that it is novel and hard to enforce, but the enforceability argument cuts less than it did a year ago, because Beijing is already moving to state-manage model exports.

**Recommended package (analyst recommendation, for ED/Under Secretary decision):** adopt 2 and 3 immediately on existing authorities; issue the §791 determination in 4; direct 5's gating conditions to US hubs and inference providers with 6 phased in for critical infrastructure within 60–90 days; hold 7 in reserve; pair all of it with the defensive measures (weight-provenance tooling, deployment guidance, CAISI evaluation cadence) because no prohibition disinfects weights already downloaded.

---

## Intelligence Gaps

1. **Where API inference actually runs.** Z.ai claims Singapore processing for the international API. We have no independent attestation of Jingsheng Hengxing's infrastructure, key custody, logging, or failover into PRC data centers. ODNI's classified annex (not yet available in this enclave) may address; **task.**
2. **Retention and access history.** No visibility into whether Z.ai logs, retains, or has disclosed API content to PRC authorities; no transparency reports exist; no known US legal process has ever tested the Singapore entity. **Task SIGINT/liaison collection.**
3. **Technical audit of GLM weights.** No USG or independent red-team evaluation has cleared GLM-5.x weights for backdoors, poisoned capabilities, or dormant triggers. CAISI has benchmarked capability, not integrity. **Task CAISI/NIST and AI security clearinghouse (EO 14409 §2(d)) for an integrity-focused evaluation.**
4. **Zhipu–PLA direct relationship.** The Recorded Future patent shows PLA adaptation of ChatGLM; we lack visibility into direct Zhipu sales, engineering support, or contracting with PLA units or defense SOEs (as opposed to open-weight reuse). **Task via Treasury/OFAC traces and IC procurement collection.**
5. **Party committee and post-IPO state seats.** Presence and role of a CCP committee inside Zhipu; board seats or reserved rights held by state investors post-IPO; identity of HK IPO cornerstone investors. Public prospectus detail not yet exploited in this product. **Task.**
6. **Precision of US exposure.** CDN telemetry is low-precision (~2,300 orgs); SBOM sampling denominators unknown; we cannot yet map which federal programs the 6 contractor integrations actually touch. **Task data team for API billing and marketplace agreement reporting.**
7. **GLM training provenance.** Whether GLM-5.x was trained or distilled in part on US-origin frontier-model outputs or US persons' data (the OSTP April 2026 memo alleges industry-scale PRC distillation generally; Zhipu's specific reliance is unassessed). **Task ODNI/Commerce.**
8. **Beijing's model-export-control end-state.** Whether Beijing will curtail, condition, or weaponize GLM's overseas availability, and on what timeline — which affects both the urgency and the durability of any US measure. **Task.**

# OICTS — ICTS Case 2026-0412: Recommended Measures
CUI//PROPIN

**Subject:** Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. d/b/a Z.ai (HKEX: 2513) — GLM-family models
**Companion product:** `assessment.md` (ICTS 2026-0412, 9 Oct 2026)
**Prepared by:** OICTS Analytic Cell | **Status:** Draft analyst recommendation for Executive Director / Under Secretary decision
**Handling:** CUI//PROPIN. Analyst recommendations only; final measures are decisions for the Department, the ERC, and where applicable the President's delegated authorities.

Each measure below is one paragraph: what it does, the authority it rides on, and the trade-offs — including the interagency equities already on record (DoD's request that open-weight use on DoD networks be addressed; CISA's supply-chain caution and its recommendation of at least guidance for federal agencies; State/EB's caution about the enforceability and diplomatic cost of prohibiting self-hosted open weights).

1. **M1 — Continued monitoring (baseline).** Keep the case open, task collection against the intelligence gaps in the companion assessment, and take no regulatory action. This maximizes optionality and avoids economic and diplomatic costs, but it concedes the data-access risk today (we can already demonstrate serving-layer prompt inspection by Z.ai and covert client-side collection by ZCode), and every quarter of inaction deepens the dependency: GLM is now a first-party listing on Amazon Bedrock and Microsoft Foundry, embedded in 41 sampled US products, six of them federal contractors. Monitoring alone is a decision to let the exposure grow while we watch. **Recommended only as a floor, not as the posture.**

2. **M2 — CISA Binding Operational Directive and federal guidance (EO 14409 §2(c)).** Direct CISA to issue a BOD requiring civilian FCEBs to inventory and block Z.ai hosted endpoints (api.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn, ZCode cloud features) on federal information systems and devices, and to publish guidance for state, local, and critical-infrastructure operators. This rides on existing delegated authority under EO 14409 (June 2026), is fast (30-day machinery already exists), and directly answers CISA's recommendation of "guidance for federal agencies at minimum." Trade-offs: it covers only federal systems, does not reach the private sector or marketplaces, and is enforcement-light — agencies self-report. It is necessary but nowhere near sufficient.

3. **M3 — FAR-based procurement restrictions for federal contractors.** Mirror NDAA FY2026 §1532's contractor prohibition in the FAR for civilian agencies: no contractor may use GLM/Z.ai services or weights in the performance of a federal contract, with required SBOM/model-provenance disclosure so agencies can see GLM inside vendor products (we found it in 41 sampled US products via SBOM, six of them federal contractors — federal agencies currently cannot see that). This is the civilian-agency analogue of what Congress already did for DoD, is enforceable through contract law and suspension/debarment, and creates real teeth because federal revenue is concentrated in the prime contractor base. Trade-offs: it does not reach commercial use outside federal contracts, imposes compliance flow-down costs on small contractors, and depends on honest disclosure — but disclosure itself changes vendor behavior, as the §1532 experience shows.

4. **M4 — ICTS determination prohibiting US-person transactions with Z.ai hosted endpoints (15 CFR part 791; EO 13873 as amended).** Issue a determination that US-person transactions involving the use of Z.ai's hosted API, platform, and associated services (api.z.ai and successors, open.bigmodel.cn, ZCode cloud functionality, and any Zhipu-controlled or successor entity, including the Singapore-registered Jingsheng Hengxing Technology Pte. Ltd.) present an undue risk, and prohibit them, subject to case-by-case authorizations. This is the decisive step against the highest-confidence threat: it stops US persons' prompts, code, and documents from flowing to PRC-controlled infrastructure, and it puts US hyperscalers and inference providers on clear legal ground to delist. It is squarely what the ICTS authorities exist for: Entity-Listing in January 2025 restricts exports *to* Zhipu but not US persons' *use* of Zhipu — a gap no other instrument closes. Trade-offs: it will cost US small and midsize developers their cheapest capable inference tier (GLM-5.x is provider-reported as competitive with US frontier models at a fraction of the price), it will not remove already-downloaded weights, and it will push some users to non-US mirrors. Those are real costs; they are lower than the cost of a PRC intelligence-accessible pipeline into thousands of US organizations.

5. **M5 — Gating conditions on US open-weight distribution channels (ICTS determination or negotiated compliance conditions).** For US model hubs and inference marketplaces (Hugging Face, OpenRouter and its listed providers, Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Cerebras, Baseten, Parasail, Novita, Featherless, and the Bedrock/Foundry listings), direct that continued commercial distribution of Zhipu-origin weights is permitted **only** under conditions: pinned cryptographic hashes of approved checkpoints with no vendor-served updates; no telemetry, update channels, or account linkage to Zhipu; no Z.ai-hosted content filters or safety layers bolted into the serving path; attestation that inference runs on US-controlled infrastructure; contractual flow-downs to end customers; and prominent PRC-provenance disclosure. This is the enforceable middle path on open weights: unlike a possession ban (see M8), distribution through identifiable commercial intermediaries can be regulated by contract, and the intermediaries are US companies who will comply. Trade-offs: it cannot stop foreign mirrors, personal downloads, or open-source reuploads elsewhere; conditions raise provider costs and will push some traffic to non-US hosts; and it leaves a PRC-origin model family seeded through US infrastructure. That residual risk is why this measure pairs with — not substitutes for — M4.

6. **M6 — Prohibition in national-security systems and designated critical infrastructure.** Designate GLM/Z.ai integration as prohibited ICTS for National Security Systems, DoD networks (already covered by NDAA §1532, which SecDef should implement so waivers are visible), and DHS-designated critical infrastructure — including the software supply chain of products sold into those environments. This addresses the worst-case pathway: a coding agent or document pipeline with PRC-origin model provenance running inside defense or critical-infrastructure networks. Trade-offs: scope definition is the hard part ("integration," "derived models," and fine-tuned variants must be defined to avoid a trivial evasion by renaming), incumbent products embedding GLM will need remediation windows, and over-inclusion sweeps in open-source-adjacent tooling that incidentally touches GLM. Sixty to ninety days for implementation via existing NSS/CNSS channels is realistic.

7. **M7 — Entity List/EAR enforcement outreach to industry.** Reissue compliance guidance making explicit what sophisticated counsel already argue (see the June 2026 compliance analysis of GLM-5.2's terms): sending US-origin controlled technical data, software source code, vulnerability data, or customer logs to Z.ai endpoints is a release to an Entity-Listed party and requires a license that will be reviewed under presumption of denial. Pair with targeted outreach to the 41 identified US integrators and their counsel, and with the 2026 CISA/NSA/FBI joint advisory already warning of PRC AI companies' industrial-scale extraction campaigns. Trade-offs: this is persuasive rather than mandatory and relies on self-reporting, but it converts an obscure export-control point into a board-level disclosure item, which is how these behaviors actually change.

8. **M8 — Prohibition on possession/self-hosting of GLM weights by US persons (reserve measure).** Prohibit US persons from downloading, hosting, or fine-tuning GLM weights. State/EB is right on the mechanics: it is legally novel (open-source code and model publication raise First Amendment and publication-precedent issues that a services ban does not), practically unenforceable at the individual level once weights are mirrored offshore, and diplomatically expensive. Two caveats sharpen the analysis: first, Beijing is itself moving to state-manage model exports (July 2026 reporting on restrictions and national-security-law penalties for model leaks), so the "reciprocity" cost of a US measure is partly prepaid — and a PRC export-control regime that curtails GLM overseas availability would strand US users with a dependency Beijing can switch off; second, enforceability improves sharply if scoped to regulated commercial intermediaries and covered sectors rather than individual possession. **Recommended posture: hold as explicit, publicly reserved escalation, pending either (a) evidence of latent compromise in GLM weights, or (b) a PRC move to curtail or weaponize GLM availability.** A reservation is only credible if it is stated.

9. **M9 — Technical integrity and defensive measures regardless of policy outcome.** Because no prohibition disinfects weights already downloaded (over 9 million cumulative downloads across zai-org repositories; GLM-5.3 at ~1.8 million within weeks of release), direct NIST/CAISI to run an integrity-focused evaluation of GLM-5.x checkpoints (beyond the capability benchmarking of 17 Sep 2026) and stand up weight-provenance verification tooling — pinned-hash manifests, reproducible-build practices for quantizations, and scanner coverage for model-serialization supply-chain risks — through the AI cybersecurity clearinghouse established under EO 14409 §2(d). This answers CISA's core caution (backdoors and poisoning "are hard to rule out") with engineering rather than assertion. Trade-offs: it will not clear a 750B-parameter artifact in any absolute sense, it consumes scarce AI-security capacity, and results must be communicated carefully (an inability to prove absence of backdoors is not proof of presence — and the same discipline must be applied to US-origin models).

10. **M10 — Coordination with Treasury, DOJ (EO 14117), and State.** Refer Z.ai API processing of US persons' personal data at scale to DOJ for the EO 14117 bulk-sensitive-data regime (28 CFR part 202), where a US-side data-broker or app developer is the transmitting party; coordinate timing with Treasury/OIA given HK-listed Zhipu paper (market cap ~US$62B) held by US index investors; and give State/EB a diplomatic track for Singapore (host of the international API's contractual processor) and for partners adopting GLM sovereign-LLM packages (ASEAN, Gulf, Africa) so that US measures do not simply relocate the exposure to allied networks. Trade-offs: interagency sequencing slows the package, and Treasury's equities (US investor exposure) cut against the most aggressive options — but acting without Treasury invites a market-disruption own goal, and acting without State concedes the BRI geographies where Zhipu is actively selling "China's answer to OpenAI for Countries."

11. **M11 — Classified integration (ODNI).** Request immediate integration of ODNI's classified annex into this case file, task the IC against the priority gaps (actual inference location for the Singapore-fronted API; retention and any PRC access history; the Zhipu–PLA relationship beyond open-weight reuse; Beijing's end-state intentions for model-export controls), and route findings into the ICTS record so the determination rests on the best available information. Trade-offs: classified product constrains interagency distribution and our ability to defend the determination publicly; a public determination built on open-source evidence is both more transparent and more robust to challenge, so the public product should stand on the open record with classified support held in reserve.

**Recommended package (analyst recommendation).** Adopt M2 and M3 immediately under existing authorities; issue the M4 ICTS determination prohibiting US-person use of Z.ai hosted endpoints as the centerpiece; impose the M5 gating conditions on US distribution channels at the same time so prohibition does not simply migrate to inference middlemen; phase M6 into national-security systems and designated critical infrastructure within 60–90 days; run M7, M9, M10, and M11 in parallel as supporting lines; and reserve M8 publicly and explicitly. The judgment behind this package is simple: Zhipu is a PRC state-directed instrument with a demonstrated record of covert data collection and a USG determination that it advances PLA military modernization — its hosted services belong out of US systems and its weights do not belong in US supply chains on Beijing's terms. The remaining policy question is not whether to act but how far the first tranche should reach; our recommendation is that it reach prohibition of the hosted service now, with the possession question held as declared, credible, and ready escalation.
